Title: FedEx advises UPS shippers to get on board now
Text: [FedEx warns UPS shippers that time is running out to switch. (Photo: Jim Allen/FreightWaves)FedEx Corp. advised shippers on Thursday that they should begin shipping now with the company if they are concerned about service disruptions arising from a possible Teamsters union strike Aug. 1 of UPS Inc.In a communique Thursday, FedEx (NYSE: FDX) said that the company’s priority is “protecting capacity and service for existing customers.” Customers considering shifting volumes to FedEx, or currently in discussions with the company to open a new account, are “encouraged to begin shipping with FedEx now,” the communique said.FedEx has said that while it has held productive discussions with UPS (NYSE: UPS) customers, it has yet to see any tangible bump in business as a result of shipper uncertainty over the situation.On Wednesday, UPS and the Teamsters broke off negotiations over a new master contract, with each side blaming the other for the breakdown. There are no new talks scheduled. The Teamsters have threatened to strike if a contract is not in hand by Aug.1, the day after the current contract expires.In an email sent Thursday to the company’s global sales and pricing teams, FedEx said that pricing offers with large customers must be signed on or before July 17 or the offer will be withdrawn. The company will honor commitments to large customers who plan to onboard after July 17.The company will bring on new small to midsize customers as it assesses network capacity. Third parties should shift business immediately as volume shipped during the week of July 17-21 will determine how much capacity will be allocated to them, FedEx said.Separately, Mike Parra, CEO of the Americas for DHL Express, the international air express unit of DHL, said Thursday that his company hasn’t benefited from shipper concern over a strike. Parra also told FreightWaves at an Atlanta event that he doesn’t want to see a strike, and that a work stoppage would lead to a “total disruption” of the U.S. economy.“There isn’t a single company on the planet that can handle 24 million shipments a day that UPS manages,” Parra said, a reference to UPS’ total daily volumes mentioned in some publications. A work stoppage would also “impact our employees, and that’s not a good thing,” Parra said.Story continues“This is not the way to earn business,” Parra said about the back and forth. “You want to earn the business the right way.”Parra was at DHL in 1997 when the Teamsters struck UPS for 15 days. “It was horrific,” he said. “We got flooded with volume, and on Day 16 all of that business went back to UPS. It impacted our loyal customers that have been there with us,” he said.The post FedEx advises UPS shippers to get on board now appeared first on FreightWaves.]

Title: PRESS DIGEST-Wall Street Journal - July 6
Text: [July 6 (Reuters) - The following are the top stories in the Wall Street Journal. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.- Facebook parent Meta Platforms on Wednesday launched Threads, a stand-alone microblogging app that takes a direct aim at Twitter as user unrest on that platform has grown since Elon Musk took the company over in October. Chief Executive Officer Mark Zuckerberg said in a post on the app that it gained 2 million sign-ups in the first two hours after its release.- JetBlue Airways said it would drop its fight in challenging a U.S. judge's ruling against a partnership with American Airlines, focusing instead on its plan to acquire Spirit Airlines for $3.8 billion, which has also been challenged by the Justice Department.- Wellful, owner of weight-loss company Nutrisystem, on Wednesday said it had acquired Jenny Craig, a defunct weight-loss brand which had shuttered in May after four decades offering personalized meal plans. While Wellful didn't disclose the purchase price, Jenny Craig's intellectual property was acquired for up to $15.5 million, according to court filings.- United Parcel Service and the International Brotherhood of Teamsters said negotiations have stalled on a new labor contract, raising the risk of roughly 330,000 workers going on strike next month. The company and the union on Wednesday each accused the other of walking away from contract talks, which have been under way since May. The current deal expires July 31.- Iran attempted to seize two oil tankers near the Strait of Hormuz and fired shots at one of them, the U.S. Navy said. In both incidents, the Iranian naval vessels left after the U.S. Navy dispatched a guided-missile destroyer to the scene, according to the U.S.'s Bahrain-based Fifth Fleet.- Most Federal Reserve officials expected they would need to lift interest rates further this year after pausing increases last month, though some wanted to raise rates in June because the economy has not slowed enough. Minutes of the June policy meeting suggest several of the 18 voting and nonvoting officials would have agreed to raise rates then. (Compiled by Bengaluru newsroom)]

Title: US labor secretary sees no need now to step into UPS-Teamsters talks
Text: [By Kanishka Singh and Nandita BoseWASHINGTON (Reuters) -Acting U.S. Labor Secretary Julie Su said on Friday she does not see a need at this stage to step in to urge parties to reach a deal in contract talks between the Teamsters Union and United Parcel Service."That is right," Su said on CNN when asked if she felt there was no need for her to intervene at this stage. She added she expected the parties to respect the bargaining process.On Wednesday, the Teamsters said UPS "walked away" from negotiations over a new contract. The company denied that and accused the union of stopping negotiating.On Friday, White House spokesperson Karine Jean-Pierre told reporters that President Joe Biden's administration was in contact with both sides and remained optimistic they would reach an agreement."I don't have any information on increased administration involvement, but certainly we remain in contact with both parties," Jean-Pierre said.The sides have traded salvos in statements as they try to avoid a strike when the current contract, which covers some 340,000 workers, expires at the end of July.If talks break down, UPS workers have already authorized a strike that would be their first since 1997. That strike lasted 15 days, cost the company $850 million, and sent some customers to rivalsBoth union and company officials have said they want a deal to prevent a strike, which could put millions of daily deliveries at risk.After missing out on wage increases during the pandemic, unions are aggressively seeking higher pay and better working conditions, pushing back on contract offers from companies grappling with labor shortages.Su recently helped negotiate a crucial contract deal between U.S. West Coast seaport employers and a union representing 22,000 workers.(Reporting by Kanishka Singh and Nandita Bose in Washington; Editing by David Holmes and David Gregorio)]

Title: Labor force is a sign of strong economy: Acting Labor Secretary
Text: [June's job report came in softer than expected, with nonfarm payrolls at 209,000, while the unemployment rate was down to 3.6%. Julie Su, Acting U.S Labor Secretary, sits down with Yahoo Finance's Jennifer Schonberger to discuss the report, unemployment, and the U.S. labor force.Su said, "This jobs report represents steady and stable growth, which is what we want in the economy."Video Transcript[MUSIC PLAYING]JENNIFER SCHONBERGER: Welcome back to Yahoo Finance Live. I'm Jennifer Schonberger. Well, with the Labor Department report coming in a bit softer than expected on that top line payroll number, 209,000 versus the 230,000 expected.But on the flip side, the unemployment rate ticking down to 3.6%. And wage growth coming in stronger than expected at 4.4%. For more analysis on this, I want to bring in acting Labor Secretary Julie Su. Secretary Su, thank you so much for joining me. It's great to be with you at the Labor Department.JULIE SU: Thank you, Jennifer. Good to be with you.JENNIFER SCHONBERGER: So we did see a little bit of softening on that top line payroll number, 209,000. And we saw some revisions downward for April and May. So we're in the 200,000 range, a bit softer than the 300,000 print we had been seeing historically. Do you think that the Fed's 10 interest rate hikes are finally starting to cool the job market?JULIE SU: Well, this is a good jobs report. This jobs report represents steady and stable growth, which is what we want in the economy, right? That is part of President Biden's economic plan, is to make sure that there is steady growth.He's helped shepherd a recovery from the pandemic-induced recession. And now, we see continued growth. And combine that with the 3.6% unemployment rate, which, you know, for the last 17 months straight, unemployment has been less than 4%.It hasn't been like that since the 1960s. And so those combined figures really demonstrate that President Biden's economic policies are working. And what we do want is that steady, stable growth, as represented by today's report.Story continuesJENNIFER SCHONBERGER: To your point, as far as strength is concerned, we saw wage growth at 4.4%, still very strong, still seeing a lot of demand for workers in this economy, especially in the services sector. How much of that strength do you think is being driven by lingering effects from the pandemic, lower immigration, early retirements? How long do you think that's going to persist?JULIE SU: That's right. So we are in a tight labor market, right? In a tight labor market, workers have more power. They have more choice. They have the ability to move from jobs to better jobs. And we've certainly seen that since the president came into office.But we've also seen a return to pre-pandemic labor force participation rates, especially in that prime-age workforce, from 25 to 54. And that is also a sign of a strong economy, of people having confidence, of people coming into labor market looking for jobs and getting jobs. And those are all good things.And we certainly see that overall, but for women, we see that women have now marked a third straight month of the highest labor force participation rate for that age group in 75 years. These are all signs of strength. It's a sign of Bidenomics, having the effect that we had. And all these things really frankly defy expectations.JENNIFER SCHONBERGER: How much longer do you think that workers are going to keep the upper hand here, and we're going to see these trends persist before the Fed finally starts to cool the job market?JULIE SU: Right. So I don't want to speak to Fed policy, right? But certainly, what we are really committed to here at the Department of Labor and across the Biden-Harris administration is making sure that additional investments are creating good jobs in every community and also bringing industry to the US, right? We're focused on manufacturing. We've had almost 800,000 manufacturing jobs created since the president came into office, and we're just getting started.We have infrastructure investments. We have semiconductor and chips. So all of these things are about delivering things for the American people and also creating good jobs in every community. And again, today's report is a sign that that kind of stable growth is not only possible, but it is actually happening under President Biden.JENNIFER SCHONBERGER: You mentioned women, women's participation in the labor force at a record high, above 77%. Yet women's wages, if you look at women versus men, they're only earning $0.83 on the dollar versus men. And we're talking about women in full-time jobs here. Why is that gap still persisting? And what can be done to really close that?JULIE SU: Yeah, thank you for mentioning that, Jennifer, because we talk about women helping to power this recovery, right? And women, as always, are doing our part. But there remain systemic issues that affect women.Obviously, some of it is care and the cost of care, something the president has talked about a lot. There's also occupational segregation that leads to the gender wage gap. And we see this moment-- and the president has been crystal clear about his commitment to equity. Leave no one behind. Make sure every community, you know, comes along in the growth that we have.And so part of it is the jobs that we're creating, we want to make sure that women have access to those jobs, that they have the training that they need to, you know, participate in manufacturing, in construction, right, in all of the growth that's happening. And so those are priorities that we have. When the president says, we need to finish the job, we have more work to do, that is part of what he means.JENNIFER SCHONBERGER: Is the president, is the administration looking to put in place any further policies to maybe help with childcare or help women who want to participate in the workforce or participate in jobs that would allow them to aspire for higher-paying positions?JULIE SU: Absolutely. So the president has called for policies, right? Like paid leave. He's indicated the importance of care work and making care both affordable and care jobs good jobs because most of those jobs are also done by women. One of the things we are focused on at the Department of Labor is creating workforce development programs, where we bring in workers and employers to focus on how we create opportunities for women.And what we've seen is when we do that, women step up, right? Women do these jobs. And it helps to close that gap.JENNIFER SCHONBERGER: Switching gears, Secretary, UPS drivers are potentially on the verge of a strike. Teamsters, the labor union that represents more than half of UPS workers, some 340,000 workers, has come to an impasse with the company. Are you prepared to intervene?Are you talking with parties at all? And if there were to be a strike, what kind of impact would we see on the job market and the economy, just given how integral UPS is to supply chains and companies that are relying on that company to get customers their products and packages?JULIE SU: Right. That's such a good point about, you know, the importance of the work that UPS workers have done and the importance of what that company's done. You know, throughout the pandemic, right, there was an increased demand for package delivery, and UPS workers stepped up to do that. I believe, as the president believes, that the collective bargaining process works, that parties coming together at the table and bargaining for wages and working conditions and benefits and the like, that that is a process that we should respect.That's a process that has historically delivered not only gains for the people at the table, but to create the middle class, right? Unions made the middle class. That's something the president says all the time. And so I have faith that the parties are going to find a path and continue to try to work things out and that there are win-win solutions, as we found when I went to the ports, to help--JENNIFER SCHONBERGER: But just standing back at this point, you're not intervening?JULIE SU: Right. We believe in the collective bargaining process, and we believe that the parties need to be given room to do what they know how to do best.JENNIFER SCHONBERGER: And before I let you go, Secretary, sticking with the union trend, the UAW, their collective bargaining agreement is set to expire with the Detroit Three automakers in mid-September. President Biden has appointed a advisor, Gene Sperling. I know he's working very closely with you. How are talks going? Are you prepared to intervene to stop any striking if it were to occur?JULIE SU: So I am working very closely with the White House. You know, this White House has been very-- this administration has been very collaborative around a whole host of issues. I think that's a premature question, right?I think the broader issue, which is consistent with jobs today, is that jobs are growing. You know, workers have come back to the labor market. And bargaining is taking place because in a tight labor market, workers have more power.And that's all a good thing because that's how we create an economy, from the bottom up, in the middle out, right? Title: The threat of a UPS strike is testing the strength of the labor market
Text: [The threat of a strike from 340,000 United Parcel Service (UPS) workers offers a new test of a recent surge in union power. It could also answer some questions about the strength of the larger US labor market.The unionized workforce at UPS was a big advantage for the package carrier earlier in the pandemic as demand for deliveries surged and rivals that lacked a steady supply of labor struggled to find enough available workers.But now that job gains are slowing and demand is cooling in some parts of the economy, it is less clear how much longer labor will hold the upper hand, either at UPS or the economy at large.New data released Friday by the Bureau of Labor Statistics showed the labor market is still tight, as the US economy added 209,000 jobs in June. That was the 30th straight month the US economy created jobs. Hourly wages also rose 4.4% over the same month last year, while the unemployment rate fell to 3.6%.But the data also showed some softening. Friday’s report marked the first in 15 months that job creation came in below what Wall Street economists had expected, reflecting a slowdown from the previous month.In the part of the economy where UPS operates — transportation and warehousing — employment actually dropped by 7,000 jobs in June.The labor market is cooling from "from overheated to lukewarm," Nancy Vanden Houten, lead US economist at Oxford Economics, said in a note on Friday.The direction of the labor market is important to the Federal Reserve as it decides whether to keep raising interest rates as a way of bringing down inflation. Officials at the central bank are watching for signs that companies are reducing hiring and wages.New wave of union activismPay is still a major issue for the International Brotherhood of Teamsters, which is pressing UPS to meet its demands for a new five-year collective bargaining agreement. It wants higher wages for the carrier’s part-time workers, among other benefits.Story continues"We need to drive up the starting rates of pay," Sean O’Brien, general president of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters, said this week on CNN.UPS has said it already offers industry-leading pay, with delivery drivers earning up to $42 per hour after four years on the job.On Wednesday, the Teamsters said the company failed to come to the table with an acceptable offer. Workers have authorized a strike to begin August 1 should no deal be reached.Sean O’Brien, general president of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters. REUTERS/Aude GuerrucciThe approach of the Teamsters is the latest sign of a new wave of union activism that took hold during the pandemic as demand for labor surged.Over the past week, Teamsters workers have expanded strikes against Amazon for delivery drivers in California and New York.The union is also testing Yellow, the nation’s third largest trucking company, to stick to the contract negotiated for its 22,000 union workers despite the company’s request to modify the agreement in efforts to avoid another bankruptcy.Amazon (AMZN), which runs its own shipping service, Amazon Logistics, has been facing unionization efforts from its warehouse workers in several states, while Apple (APPL) and Starbuck (SBUX) have been countering union pressure from retail workers.Is this 'a temporary or fundamental change'?Strikes that can jolt the nation’s supply chains are economic risks that the Biden administration has proven it is not willing to take.Over the past year, the administration has intervened in the dispute between West Coast Ports and the Dockworkers Union, and tapped Congress to settle differences between railroad companies and a dozen unions backing railway conductors. It is also monitoring talks between the auto companies and the United Auto Workers.Julie Su, acting Labor Secretary, said the White House does not plan to intervene in the UPS talks. (AP Photo/Alex Brandon, File)"All of a sudden we find ourselves in a situation we really haven’t experienced for some time," labor and employment expert and Penn State University law professor Paul Clark told Yahoo Finance."The big question is whether this is a temporary or fundamental change between unions and employers. We are trying to answer that right now, and it’s pretty difficult to say."Wayne State University labor law professor Michael Oswalt said even small disruptions in transportation, shipping and warehousing can be devastating across multiple industries. Still, he said, absent changes to labor law, which governs union campaigns and elections, unions are unlikely to regain the power they once had."So today what can matter more than a union’s size is its proximity to a company’s choke-point – and especially its willingness to strike," Oswalt said. "UPS Teamsters know the value they bring to the company, to the broader economy, and they have a history of pulling off successful strikes. That trifecta equates to a lot of union power right now."In January, the BLS reported that 10.1% of wage and salary workers belonged to unions in 2022, down from 10.3% in 2021. In the same timeframe the number of wage and salary workers who belonged to unions increased 1.9% or 273,000 workers. The total number of workers belonging to unions in 1983, according to BLS was around 20.1%, nearly double what it is today.Acting US Labor Secretary Julie Su told Yahoo Finance on Friday that the White House does not plan to intervene in the UPS situation.“I have faith that the parties are going to find a path and continue to try to work things out,” she said Friday.Jennifer Schonberger, Josh Shafer and Jared Mitovich contributed to this report.Click here for the latest stock market news and in-depth analysis, including events that move stocksRead the latest financial and business news from Yahoo Finance]

Title: US labor secretary sees no need now to step into UPS-Teamsters talks
Text: [By Kanishka Singh and Nandita BoseWASHINGTON (Reuters) -Acting U.S. Labor Secretary Julie Su said on Friday she does not see a need at this stage to step in to urge parties to reach a deal in contract talks between the Teamsters Union and United Parcel Service."That is right," Su said on CNN when asked if she felt there was no need for her to intervene at this stage. She added she expected the parties to respect the bargaining process.On Wednesday, the Teamsters said UPS "walked away" from negotiations over a new contract. The company denied that and accused the union of stopping negotiating.On Friday, White House spokesperson Karine Jean-Pierre told reporters that President Joe Biden's administration was in contact with both sides and remained optimistic they would reach an agreement."I don't have any information on increased administration involvement, but certainly we remain in contact with both parties," Jean-Pierre said.The sides have traded salvos in statements as they try to avoid a strike when the current contract, which covers some 340,000 workers, expires at the end of July.If talks break down, UPS workers have already authorized a strike that would be their first since 1997. That strike lasted 15 days, cost the company $850 million, and sent some customers to rivalsBoth union and company officials have said they want a deal to prevent a strike, which could put millions of daily deliveries at risk.After missing out on wage increases during the pandemic, unions are aggressively seeking higher pay and better working conditions, pushing back on contract offers from companies grappling with labor shortages.Su recently helped negotiate a crucial contract deal between U.S. West Coast seaport employers and a union representing 22,000 workers.(Reporting by Kanishka Singh and Nandita Bose in Washington; Editing by David Holmes and David Gregorio)]

Title: Labor force is a sign of strong economy: Acting Labor Secretary
Text: [June's job report came in softer than expected, with nonfarm payrolls at 209,000, while the unemployment rate was down to 3.6%. Julie Su, Acting U.S Labor Secretary, sits down with Yahoo Finance's Jennifer Schonberger to discuss the report, unemployment, and the U.S. labor force.Su said, "This jobs report represents steady and stable growth, which is what we want in the economy."Video Transcript[MUSIC PLAYING]JENNIFER SCHONBERGER: Welcome back to Yahoo Finance Live. I'm Jennifer Schonberger. Well, with the Labor Department report coming in a bit softer than expected on that top line payroll number, 209,000 versus the 230,000 expected.But on the flip side, the unemployment rate ticking down to 3.6%. And wage growth coming in stronger than expected at 4.4%. For more analysis on this, I want to bring in acting Labor Secretary Julie Su. Secretary Su, thank you so much for joining me. It's great to be with you at the Labor Department.JULIE SU: Thank you, Jennifer. Good to be with you.JENNIFER SCHONBERGER: So we did see a little bit of softening on that top line payroll number, 209,000. And we saw some revisions downward for April and May. So we're in the 200,000 range, a bit softer than the 300,000 print we had been seeing historically. Do you think that the Fed's 10 interest rate hikes are finally starting to cool the job market?JULIE SU: Well, this is a good jobs report. This jobs report represents steady and stable growth, which is what we want in the economy, right? That is part of President Biden's economic plan, is to make sure that there is steady growth.He's helped shepherd a recovery from the pandemic-induced recession. And now, we see continued growth. And combine that with the 3.6% unemployment rate, which, you know, for the last 17 months straight, unemployment has been less than 4%.It hasn't been like that since the 1960s. And so those combined figures really demonstrate that President Biden's economic policies are working. And what we do want is that steady, stable growth, as represented by today's report.Story continuesJENNIFER SCHONBERGER: To your point, as far as strength is concerned, we saw wage growth at 4.4%, still very strong, still seeing a lot of demand for workers in this economy, especially in the services sector. How much of that strength do you think is being driven by lingering effects from the pandemic, lower immigration, early retirements? How long do you think that's going to persist?JULIE SU: That's right. So we are in a tight labor market, right? In a tight labor market, workers have more power. They have more choice. They have the ability to move from jobs to better jobs. And we've certainly seen that since the president came into office.But we've also seen a return to pre-pandemic labor force participation rates, especially in that prime-age workforce, from 25 to 54. And that is also a sign of a strong economy, of people having confidence, of people coming into labor market looking for jobs and getting jobs. And those are all good things.And we certainly see that overall, but for women, we see that women have now marked a third straight month of the highest labor force participation rate for that age group in 75 years. These are all signs of strength. It's a sign of Bidenomics, having the effect that we had. And all these things really frankly defy expectations.JENNIFER SCHONBERGER: How much longer do you think that workers are going to keep the upper hand here, and we're going to see these trends persist before the Fed finally starts to cool the job market?JULIE SU: Right. So I don't want to speak to Fed policy, right? But certainly, what we are really committed to here at the Department of Labor and across the Biden-Harris administration is making sure that additional investments are creating good jobs in every community and also bringing industry to the US, right? We're focused on manufacturing. We've had almost 800,000 manufacturing jobs created since the president came into office, and we're just getting started.We have infrastructure investments. We have semiconductor and chips. So all of these things are about delivering things for the American people and also creating good jobs in every community. And again, today's report is a sign that that kind of stable growth is not only possible, but it is actually happening under President Biden.JENNIFER SCHONBERGER: You mentioned women, women's participation in the labor force at a record high, above 77%. Yet women's wages, if you look at women versus men, they're only earning $0.83 on the dollar versus men. And we're talking about women in full-time jobs here. Why is that gap still persisting? And what can be done to really close that?JULIE SU: Yeah, thank you for mentioning that, Jennifer, because we talk about women helping to power this recovery, right? And women, as always, are doing our part. But there remain systemic issues that affect women.Obviously, some of it is care and the cost of care, something the president has talked about a lot. There's also occupational segregation that leads to the gender wage gap. And we see this moment-- and the president has been crystal clear about his commitment to equity. Leave no one behind. Make sure every community, you know, comes along in the growth that we have.And so part of it is the jobs that we're creating, we want to make sure that women have access to those jobs, that they have the training that they need to, you know, participate in manufacturing, in construction, right, in all of the growth that's happening. And so those are priorities that we have. When the president says, we need to finish the job, we have more work to do, that is part of what he means.JENNIFER SCHONBERGER: Is the president, is the administration looking to put in place any further policies to maybe help with childcare or help women who want to participate in the workforce or participate in jobs that would allow them to aspire for higher-paying positions?JULIE SU: Absolutely. So the president has called for policies, right? Like paid leave. He's indicated the importance of care work and making care both affordable and care jobs good jobs because most of those jobs are also done by women. One of the things we are focused on at the Department of Labor is creating workforce development programs, where we bring in workers and employers to focus on how we create opportunities for women.And what we've seen is when we do that, women step up, right? Women do these jobs. And it helps to close that gap.JENNIFER SCHONBERGER: Switching gears, Secretary, UPS drivers are potentially on the verge of a strike. Teamsters, the labor union that represents more than half of UPS workers, some 340,000 workers, has come to an impasse with the company. Are you prepared to intervene?Are you talking with parties at all? And if there were to be a strike, what kind of impact would we see on the job market and the economy, just given how integral UPS is to supply chains and companies that are relying on that company to get customers their products and packages?JULIE SU: Right. That's such a good point about, you know, the importance of the work that UPS workers have done and the importance of what that company's done. You know, throughout the pandemic, right, there was an increased demand for package delivery, and UPS workers stepped up to do that. I believe, as the president believes, that the collective bargaining process works, that parties coming together at the table and bargaining for wages and working conditions and benefits and the like, that that is a process that we should respect.That's a process that has historically delivered not only gains for the people at the table, but to create the middle class, right? Unions made the middle class. That's something the president says all the time. And so I have faith that the parties are going to find a path and continue to try to work things out and that there are win-win solutions, as we found when I went to the ports, to help--JENNIFER SCHONBERGER: But just standing back at this point, you're not intervening?JULIE SU: Right. We believe in the collective bargaining process, and we believe that the parties need to be given room to do what they know how to do best.JENNIFER SCHONBERGER: And before I let you go, Secretary, sticking with the union trend, the UAW, their collective bargaining agreement is set to expire with the Detroit Three automakers in mid-September. President Biden has appointed a advisor, Gene Sperling. I know he's working very closely with you. How are talks going? Are you prepared to intervene to stop any striking if it were to occur?JULIE SU: So I am working very closely with the White House. You know, this White House has been very-- this administration has been very collaborative around a whole host of issues. I think that's a premature question, right?I think the broader issue, which is consistent with jobs today, is that jobs are growing. You know, workers have come back to the labor market. And bargaining is taking place because in a tight labor market, workers have more power.And that's all a good thing because that's how we create an economy, from the bottom up, in the middle out, right? That's how we make sure that every job is a good job. That's how we make sure that we honor what workers have done and their power in the workplace. And, you know, I think those are all part of the Bidenomics vision of what makes a good strong economy.JENNIFER SCHONBERGER: Secretary Su, thank you so much for your insight. It was great to have you on the program.JULIE SU: Thank you so much, Jennifer.JENNIFER SCHONBERGER: I hope to speak with you again soon. Thank you me too.]

Title: The threat of a UPS strike is testing the strength of the labor market
Text: [The threat of a strike from 340,000 United Parcel Service (UPS) workers offers a new test of a recent surge in union power. It could also answer some questions about the strength of the larger US labor market.The unionized workforce at UPS was a big advantage for the package carrier earlier in the pandemic as demand for deliveries surged and rivals that lacked a steady supply of labor struggled to find enough available workers.But now that job gains are slowing and demand is cooling in some parts of the economy, it is less clear how much longer labor will hold the upper hand, either at UPS or the economy at large.New data released Friday by the Bureau of Labor Statistics showed the labor market is still tight, as the US economy added 209,000 jobs in June. That was the 30th straight month the US economy created jobs. Hourly wages also rose 4.4% over the same month last year, while the unemployment rate fell to 3.6%.But the data also showed some softening. Friday’s report marked the first in 15 months that job creation came in below what Wall Street economists had expected, reflecting a slowdown from the previous month.In the part of the economy where UPS operates — transportation and warehousing — employment actually dropped by 7,000 jobs in June.The labor market is cooling from "from overheated to lukewarm," Nancy Vanden Houten, lead US economist at Oxford Economics, said in a note on Friday.The direction of the labor market is important to the Federal Reserve as it decides whether to keep raising interest rates as a way of bringing down inflation. Officials at the central bank are watching for signs that companies are reducing hiring and wages.New wave of union activismPay is still a major issue for the International Brotherhood of Teamsters, which is pressing UPS to meet its demands for a new five-year collective bargaining agreement. It wants higher wages for the carrier’s part-time workers, among other benefits.Story continues"We need to drive up the starting rates of pay," Sean O’Brien, general president of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters, said this week on CNN.UPS has said it already offers industry-leading pay, with delivery drivers earning up to $42 per hour after four years on the job.On Wednesday, the Teamsters said the company failed to come to the table with an acceptable offer. Workers have authorized a strike to begin August 1 should no deal be reached.Sean O’Brien, general president of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters. REUTERS/Aude GuerrucciThe approach of the Teamsters is the latest sign of a new wave of union activism that took hold during the pandemic as demand for labor surged.Over the past week, Teamsters workers have expanded strikes against Amazon for delivery drivers in California and New York.The union is also testing Yellow, the nation’s third largest trucking company, to stick to the contract negotiated for its 22,000 union workers despite the company’s request to modify the agreement in efforts to avoid another bankruptcy.Amazon (AMZN), which runs its own shipping service, Amazon Logistics, has been facing unionization efforts from its warehouse workers in several states, while Apple (APPL) and Starbuck (SBUX) have been countering union pressure from retail workers.Is this 'a temporary or fundamental change'?Strikes that can jolt the nation’s supply chains are economic risks that the Biden administration has proven it is not willing to take.Over the past year, the administration has intervened in the dispute between West Coast Ports and the Dockworkers Union, and tapped Congress to settle differences between railroad companies and a dozen unions backing railway conductors. It is also monitoring talks between the auto companies and the United Auto Workers.Julie Su, acting Labor Secretary, said the White House does not plan to intervene in the UPS talks. (AP Photo/Alex Brandon, File)"All of a sudden we find ourselves in a situation we really haven’t experienced for some time," labor and employment expert and Penn State University law professor Paul Clark told Yahoo Finance."The big question is whether this is a temporary or fundamental change between unions and employers. We are trying to answer that right now, and it’s pretty difficult to say."Wayne State University labor law professor Michael Oswalt said even small disruptions in transportation, shipping and warehousing can be devastating across multiple industries. Still, he said, absent changes to labor law, which governs union campaigns and elections, unions are unlikely to regain the power they once had."So today what can matter more than a union’s size is its proximity to a company’s choke-point – and especially its willingness to strike," Oswalt said. "UPS Teamsters know the value they bring to the company, to the broader economy, and they have a history of pulling off successful strikes. That trifecta equates to a lot of union power right now."In January, the BLS reported that 10.1% of wage and salary workers belonged to unions in 2022, down from 10.3% in 2021. In the same timeframe the number of wage and salary workers who belonged to unions increased 1.9% or 273,000 workers. The total number of workers belonging to unions in 1983, according to BLS was around 20.1%, nearly double what it is today.Acting US Labor Secretary Julie Su told Yahoo Finance on Friday that the White House does not plan to intervene in the UPS situation.“I have faith that the parties are going to find a path and continue to try to work things out,” she said Friday.Jennifer Schonberger, Josh Shafer and Jared Mitovich contributed to this report.Click here for the latest stock market news and in-depth analysis, including events that move stocksRead the latest financial and business news from Yahoo Finance]

Title: US labor secretary sees no need now to step into UPS-Teamsters talks
Text: [By Kanishka Singh and Nandita BoseWASHINGTON (Reuters) -Acting U.S. Labor Secretary Julie Su said on Friday she does not see a need at this stage to step in to urge parties to reach a deal in contract talks between the Teamsters Union and United Parcel Service."That is right," Su said on CNN when asked if she felt there was no need for her to intervene at this stage. She added she expected the parties to respect the bargaining process.On Wednesday, the Teamsters said UPS "walked away" from negotiations over a new contract. The company denied that and accused the union of stopping negotiating.On Friday, White House spokesperson Karine Jean-Pierre told reporters that President Joe Biden's administration was in contact with both sides and remained optimistic they would reach an agreement."I don't have any information on increased administration involvement, but certainly we remain in contact with both parties," Jean-Pierre said.The sides have traded salvos in statements as they try to avoid a strike when the current contract, which covers some 340,000 workers, expires at the end of July.If talks break down, UPS workers have already authorized a strike that would be their first since 1997. That strike lasted 15 days, cost the company $850 million, and sent some customers to rivalsBoth union and company officials have said they want a deal to prevent a strike, which could put millions of daily deliveries at risk.After missing out on wage increases during the pandemic, unions are aggressively seeking higher pay and better working conditions, pushing back on contract offers from companies grappling with labor shortages.Su recently helped negotiate a crucial contract deal between U.S. West Coast seaport employers and a union representing 22,000 workers.(Reporting by Kanishka Singh and Nandita Bose in Washington; Editing by David Holmes and David Gregorio)]

Title: Labor force is a sign of strong economy: Acting Labor Secretary
Text: [June's job report came in softer than expected, with nonfarm payrolls at 209,000, while the unemployment rate was down to 3.6%. Julie Su, Acting U.S Labor Secretary, sits down with Yahoo Finance's Jennifer Schonberger to discuss the report, unemployment, and the U.S. labor force.Su said, "This jobs report represents steady and stable growth, which is what we want in the economy."Video Transcript[MUSIC PLAYING]JENNIFER SCHONBERGER: Welcome back to Yahoo Finance Live. I'm Jennifer Schonberger. Well, with the Labor Department report coming in a bit softer than expected on that top line payroll number, 209,000 versus the 230,000 expected.But on the flip side, the unemployment rate ticking down to 3.6%. And wage growth coming in stronger than expected at 4.4%. For more analysis on this, I want to bring in acting Labor Secretary Julie Su. Secretary Su, thank you so much for joining me. It's great to be with you at the Labor Department.JULIE SU: Thank you, Jennifer. Good to be with you.JENNIFER SCHONBERGER: So we did see a little bit of softening on that top line payroll number, 209,000. And we saw some revisions downward for April and May. So we're in the 200,000 range, a bit softer than the 300,000 print we had been seeing historically. Do you think that the Fed's 10 interest rate hikes are finally starting to cool the job market?JULIE SU: Well, this is a good jobs report. This jobs report represents steady and stable growth, which is what we want in the economy, right? That is part of President Biden's economic plan, is to make sure that there is steady growth.He's helped shepherd a recovery from the pandemic-induced recession. And now, we see continued growth. And combine that with the 3.6% unemployment rate, which, you know, for the last 17 months straight, unemployment has been less than 4%.It hasn't been like that since the 1960s. And so those combined figures really demonstrate that President Biden's economic policies are working. And what we do want is that steady, stable growth, as represented by today's report.Story continuesJENNIFER SCHONBERGER: To your point, as far as strength is concerned, we saw wage growth at 4.4%, still very strong, still seeing a lot of demand for workers in this economy, especially in the services sector. How much of that strength do you think is being driven by lingering effects from the pandemic, lower immigration, early retirements? How long do you think that's going to persist?JULIE SU: That's right. So we are in a tight labor market, right? In a tight labor market, workers have more power. They have more choice. They have the ability to move from jobs to better jobs. And we've certainly seen that since the president came into office.But we've also seen a return to pre-pandemic labor force participation rates, especially in that prime-age workforce, from 25 to 54. And that is also a sign of a strong economy, of people having confidence, of people coming into labor market looking for jobs and getting jobs. And those are all good things.And we certainly see that overall, but for women, we see that women have now marked a third straight month of the highest labor force participation rate for that age group in 75 years. These are all signs of strength. It's a sign of Bidenomics, having the effect that we had. And all these things really frankly defy expectations.JENNIFER SCHONBERGER: How much longer do you think that workers are going to keep the upper hand here, and we're going to see these trends persist before the Fed finally starts to cool the job market?JULIE SU: Right. So I don't want to speak to Fed policy, right? But certainly, what we are really committed to here at the Department of Labor and across the Biden-Harris administration is making sure that additional investments are creating good jobs in every community and also bringing industry to the US, right? We're focused on manufacturing. We've had almost 800,000 manufacturing jobs created since the president came into office, and we're just getting started.We have infrastructure investments. We have semiconductor and chips. So all of these things are about delivering things for the American people and also creating good jobs in every community. And again, today's report is a sign that that kind of stable growth is not only possible, but it is actually happening under President Biden.JENNIFER SCHONBERGER: You mentioned women, women's participation in the labor force at a record high, above 77%. Yet women's wages, if you look at women versus men, they're only earning $0.83 on the dollar versus men. And we're talking about women in full-time jobs here. Why is that gap still persisting? And what can be done to really close that?JULIE SU: Yeah, thank you for mentioning that, Jennifer, because we talk about women helping to power this recovery, right? And women, as always, are doing our part. But there remain systemic issues that affect women.Obviously, some of it is care and the cost of care, something the president has talked about a lot. There's also occupational segregation that leads to the gender wage gap. And we see this moment-- and the president has been crystal clear about his commitment to equity. Leave no one behind. Make sure every community, you know, comes along in the growth that we have.And so part of it is the jobs that we're creating, we want to make sure that women have access to those jobs, that they have the training that they need to, you know, participate in manufacturing, in construction, right, in all of the growth that's happening. And so those are priorities that we have. When the president says, we need to finish the job, we have more work to do, that is part of what he means.JENNIFER SCHONBERGER: Is the president, is the administration looking to put in place any further policies to maybe help with childcare or help women who want to participate in the workforce or participate in jobs that would allow them to aspire for higher-paying positions?JULIE SU: Absolutely. So the president has called for policies, right? Like paid leave. He's indicated the importance of care work and making care both affordable and care jobs good jobs because most of those jobs are also done by women. One of the things we are focused on at the Department of Labor is creating workforce development programs, where we bring in workers and employers to focus on how we create opportunities for women.And what we've seen is when we do that, women step up, right? Women do these jobs. And it helps to close that gap.JENNIFER SCHONBERGER: Switching gears, Secretary, UPS drivers are potentially on the verge of a strike. Teamsters, the labor union that represents more than half of UPS workers, some 340,000 workers, has come to an impasse with the company. Are you prepared to intervene?Are you talking with parties at all? And if there were to be a strike, what kind of impact would we see on the job market and the economy, just given how integral UPS is to supply chains and companies that are relying on that company to get customers their products and packages?JULIE SU: Right. That's such a good point about, you know, the importance of the work that UPS workers have done and the importance of what that company's done. You know, throughout the pandemic, right, there was an increased demand for package delivery, and UPS workers stepped up to do that. I believe, as the president believes, that the collective bargaining process works, that parties coming together at the table and bargaining for wages and working conditions and benefits and the like, that that is a process that we should respect.That's a process that has historically delivered not only gains for the people at the table, but to create the middle class, right? Unions made the middle class. That's something the president says all the time. And so I have faith that the parties are going to find a path and continue to try to work things out and that there are win-win solutions, as we found when I went to the ports, to help--JENNIFER SCHONBERGER: But just standing back at this point, you're not intervening?JULIE SU: Right. We believe in the collective bargaining process, and we believe that the parties need to be given room to do what they know how to do best.JENNIFER SCHONBERGER: And before I let you go, Secretary, sticking with the union trend, the UAW, their collective bargaining agreement is set to expire with the Detroit Three automakers in mid-September. President Biden has appointed a advisor, Gene Sperling. I know he's working very closely with you. How are talks going? Are you prepared to intervene to stop any striking if it were to occur?JULIE SU: So I am working very closely with the White House. You know, this White House has been very-- this administration has been very collaborative around a whole host of issues. I think that's a premature question, right?I think the broader issue, which is consistent with jobs today, is that jobs are growing. You know, workers have come back to the labor market. And bargaining is taking place because in a tight labor market, workers have more power.And that's all a good thing because that's how we create an economy, from the bottom up, in the middle out, right? That's how we make sure that every job is a good job. That's how we make sure that we honor what workers have done and their power in the workplace. And, you know, I think those are all part of the Bidenomics vision of what makes a good strong economy.JENNIFER SCHONBERGER: Secretary Su, thank you so much for your insight. It was great to have you on the program.JULIE SU: Thank you so much, Jennifer.JENNIFER SCHONBERGER: I hope to speak with you again soon. Thank you me too.]

Title: Consultant: Strike could cost UPS 30% of diverted volume
Text: [UPS could see 30% of diverted volume disappear, consultant says (Photo: Jim Allen/FreightWaves)UPS Inc. should be prepared to lose as much as 30% of diverted volume should the Teamsters strike the company by the end of the month and a work stoppage last for a decent duration, a leading parcel consultant said Monday.UPS handled about 18.6 million parcels in the U.S. per day in the first quarter. Under a contingency plan, it expects to handle 4 million parcels on its own. The balance of about 14.6 million parcels, most of which would be ground deliveries, would be subject to diversion.Satish Jindel, president of consultancy ShipMatrix, said in a communique to FreightWaves that the 30% of volume that could be lost would be equivalent to more than 4 million parcels a day.Because there are about 80,000 package car drivers and each driver delivers about 230 parcels per day, the diverted volume, if it never returns to UPS (NYSE: UPS), could result in 4,300 lost driver jobs and those of a few thousand package handlers for every 1 million packages diverted, he said.Unlike the last Teamster strike in 1997, there is plenty of competition for diverted volume. For example, FedEx Corp., (NYSE: FDX) whose ground unit didn’t exist back then, is delivering on-time performance for air and ground on par with UPS, according to Jindel. This will give shippers more confidence to keep diverted volumes with FedEx, he said.On Sunday, the U.S. Postal Service launched “Ground Advantage” with two-to-five-day transit times comparable to FedEx and UPS. Jindel envisioned a scenario in which large shippers divert lightweight parcels under 5 pounds that can fit in a mailbox to the Postal Service and the heavier parcels to FedEx.The potential damage to UPS and its unionized workers behooves both sides to return to the table and resume negotiations, Jindel said. Talks collapsed last week reportedly over an inability to come to terms on part-time wages. No new talks are scheduled. The current contract expires July 31.“Being very tough in negotiations is analogous to stretching a rubber band,” Jindel wrote. “No one knows the full limit before it snaps and then one has to start all over again with a new set of conditions.”Story continuesSeparately, for the minority of Teamsters union members at UPS who don’t favor a strike should a contract not be agreed to in three weeks, the National Right to Work Legal Defense Foundation on Monday issued some advice.All UPS employees can resign their membership in the union and continue to do their jobs, according to a legal notice issued by the foundation. “If you don’t support the union you can send the union a letter resigning your membership at any time,” the notice said.In addition, employees who resign their membership — or who are already nonmembers — have the right to work even if the union orders a strike. “Union officials can — and often do — fine union members thousands of dollars for working during a strike,” the notice said. “So you should seriously consider resigning your union membership before you return to work during a strike, which is the only way to avoid fines and discipline.”Employees working in a “right-to-work” state, where union membership and financial support are voluntary, can resign their membership and opt out of all union financial support, according to the notice.Employees not working in a state with those protections have the right to opt out of paying dues for union politics and may be able to avoid other union financial support, according to the notice. In non-right-to-work states, unions can still only mandate that employees pay dues as a condition of employment if the union and management have finalized a union monopoly bargaining contract that contains a valid forced-dues clause, the notice said.About 97% of UPS’ members have voted to authorize a strike if a contract is not reached by July 31. The Teamsters represent 340,000 UPS employees, many of them part-timers.The post Consultant: Strike could cost UPS 30% of diverted volume appeared first on FreightWaves.]

Title: Amazon Prime Day: How a potential UPS strike could boost sales
Text: [Amazon's Prime Day sales event kicks off on Tuesday. Burt Flickinger, Managing Director at Strategic Resource Group, tells Yahoo Finance Live how the e-commerce giant could see a bump in sales due to concerns about a potential strike by UPS workers.Video TranscriptSEANA SMITH: Amazon's Prime Day kicks off tomorrow, July 11th. And our next guest is expecting strong sales and deep discounts. For more on what to expect, we want to bring in Burt Flickinger. He's Strategic Resource Group Managing Director.Burt, it's good to see you. So there has been this ongoing debate about the health of the consumer, the consensus of the consumer right now given all the headwinds. What do you think Prime Day is going to tell us just about where the consumer stands today?BURT FLICKINGER: Prime Day is going to tell us that the consumer is looking for the best bargains in history, because 64% of Americans are living paycheck to paycheck. Food stamps or SNAP benefits have just been cut significantly.Post-COVID and travel is getting more expensive and more difficult as AAA's reported record travel delays during the 4th of July holiday week in the US and Canada. So people want affordable luxuries. And they'll be able to afford more of them with Amazon Prime Day this week, as you said, tomorrow and the following day.AKIKO FUJITA: Yeah, interesting that you mentioned that the weakness and some of the headwinds that consumers face are actually going to lead to a big bump for Amazon.The other thing that you've said you're watching very closely is this UPS strike. I'm curious to hear what you think about that and how that's going to give a bump, because is that necessarily what consumers are watching right now?BURT FLICKINGER: Consumers are watching it because you and other worldwide networks are reporting it so well. UPS represents about 35%, 37% of Amazon's shipments, but it also represents shipments to hundreds of different retailers in LTL or less-than-truckload.Story continuesAnd the Teamsters have not struck Amazon since 1997 good-- or struck UPS delivering for Amazon since 1997. But the Teamsters have a dynamic new leader, Sean O'Brien, who does not do contract extensions and will not settle with the Hoffa family settled for was 2% to 3% annual wage increases. So we expect a work stoppage.Consumers expect the same thing so consumers will buy in advance to get back to school or back to school essentials-- shoes, clothes, books, and supplies-- to make sure there's something when the kids go back to school next month in August.SEANA SMITH: So, Burt, you're saying consumers are closely paying attention to this. And maybe you slightly inserted there. But more specifically, I guess, what are retailers doing? Are they ordering ahead? What changes are they making to their supply chains in anticipation or to better position themselves if we do see a strike?BURT FLICKINGER: Our retailers are ordering ahead. And they're caught between the proverbial Scylla and Charybdis, because they're just coming off of what you and Akiko reported so well in terms of the supply chain shortages for over 1,000 days.They're just finding their footing from that. And now they have to advance shipments because of the potential UPS Teamsters strike. Full disclosure, I was a member of the Teamsters as a second job, working my way through high school and college and road delivery. And when they're off the road, the national economy really gets crushed.AKIKO FUJITA: Burt, so let's talk about what exactly the deals are going to look like. Because as you point out the last Prime Day in the fall was a bit of a disappointment when you compare it to how things were in July. So how significant do you anticipate the discounts to be, and where will they be focused on?BURT FLICKINGER: Akiko, great insights as usual. And the discounts will be primarily consumer electronics, consumer audio, and especially tech. And as you referenced, Amazon did about $12 billion in Prime Day last July. But in Prime Days in October, did about 8 billion.Meanwhile Alibaba worldwide did about $40 billion in one day, November 11th in 2022. So Amazon's got to, one, close the gap versus Alibaba. Two, close the deficit from last October that you referenced.And, third, close the gap that Whole Foods has been disappointing since the acquisition in 2017, and they have to offset those sideways sales and land-based retail with more Amazon e-tail and to coincide with the tremendous press of Amazon growth of AWS or Amazon Web Services to your good points.SEANA SMITH: Burt, what about the resumption of student loan payments? We know investors are keeping a close eye on that. Just on what this means for other retailers, but what it means for Prime Day. Is that something that you expect to affect this year's event or it's something that you see more of affecting 2024 Prime Day?BURT FLICKINGER: Seana, expect to affect Prime Day this year. And one thing I missed is Amazon's really going to focus on both wearables and electronics as well as consumables.It's the path to growth, because consumers are paying the highest prices in history-- especially the highest prices in food-- so Amazon online is going to really accelerate and challenge Kroger, Albertsons Walmart, Costco target who all have the majority of their sales in consumable food and beverage and other consumable categories.Amazon's really going to step up this year. So one can stock his or her entire apartment or home with edibles, wearables, and everything for electronics and technology too.SEANA SMITH: Well, we will see what those sales numbers look like. Burt Flickinger, thanks.]

Title: U.S. Postal Service Wants More Packages to Wrest Business From UPS, FedEx
The threat of a UPS strike is testing the strength of the labor market
Text: [The threat of a strike from 340,000 United Parcel Service (UPS) workers offers a new test of a recent surge in union power. It could also answer some questions about the strength of the larger US labor market.The unionized workforce at UPS was a big advantage for the package carrier earlier in the pandemic as demand for deliveries surged and rivals that lacked a steady supply of labor struggled to find enough available workers.But now that job gains are slowing and demand is cooling in some parts of the economy, it is less clear how much longer labor will hold the upper hand, either at UPS or the economy at large.New data released Friday by the Bureau of Labor Statistics showed the labor market is still tight, as the US economy added 209,000 jobs in June. That was the 30th straight month the US economy created jobs. Hourly wages also rose 4.4% over the same month last year, while the unemployment rate fell to 3.6%.But the data also showed some softening. Friday’s report marked the first in 15 months that job creation came in below what Wall Street economists had expected, reflecting a slowdown from the previous month.In the part of the economy where UPS operates — transportation and warehousing — employment actually dropped by 7,000 jobs in June.The labor market is cooling from "from overheated to lukewarm," Nancy Vanden Houten, lead US economist at Oxford Economics, said in a note on Friday.The direction of the labor market is important to the Federal Reserve as it decides whether to keep raising interest rates as a way of bringing down inflation. Officials at the central bank are watching for signs that companies are reducing hiring and wages.New wave of union activismPay is still a major issue for the International Brotherhood of Teamsters, which is pressing UPS to meet its demands for a new five-year collective bargaining agreement. It wants higher wages for the carrier’s part-time workers, among other benefits.Story continues"We need to drive up the starting rates of pay," Sean O’Brien, general president of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters, said this week on CNN.UPS has said it already offers industry-leading pay, with delivery drivers earning up to $42 per hour after four years on the job.On Wednesday, the Teamsters said the company failed to come to the table with an acceptable offer. Workers have authorized a strike to begin August 1 should no deal be reached.Sean O’Brien, general president of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters. REUTERS/Aude GuerrucciThe approach of the Teamsters is the latest sign of a new wave of union activism that took hold during the pandemic as demand for labor surged.Over the past week, Teamsters workers have expanded strikes against Amazon for delivery drivers in California and New York.The union is also testing Yellow, the nation’s third largest trucking company, to stick to the contract negotiated for its 22,000 union workers despite the company’s request to modify the agreement in efforts to avoid another bankruptcy.Amazon (AMZN), which runs its own shipping service, Amazon Logistics, has been facing unionization efforts from its warehouse workers in several states, while Apple (APPL) and Starbuck (SBUX) have been countering union pressure from retail workers.Is this 'a temporary or fundamental change'?Strikes that can jolt the nation’s supply chains are economic risks that the Biden administration has proven it is not willing to take.Over the past year, the administration has intervened in the dispute between West Coast Ports and the Dockworkers Union, and tapped Congress to settle differences between railroad companies and a dozen unions backing railway conductors. It is also monitoring talks between the auto companies and the United Auto Workers.Julie Su, acting Labor Secretary, said the White House does not plan to intervene in the UPS talks. (AP Photo/Alex Brandon, File)"All of a sudden we find ourselves in a situation we really haven’t experienced for some time," labor and employment expert and Penn State University law professor Paul Clark told Yahoo Finance."The big question is whether this is a temporary or fundamental change between unions and employers. We are trying to answer that right now, and it’s pretty difficult to say."Wayne State University labor law professor Michael Oswalt said even small disruptions in transportation, shipping and warehousing can be devastating across multiple industries. Still, he said, absent changes to labor law, which governs union campaigns and elections, unions are unlikely to regain the power they once had."So today what can matter more than a union’s size is its proximity to a company’s choke-point – and especially its willingness to strike," Oswalt said. "UPS Teamsters know the value they bring to the company, to the broader economy, and they have a history of pulling off successful strikes. That trifecta equates to a lot of union power right now."In January, the BLS reported that 10.1% of wage and salary workers belonged to unions in 2022, down from 10.3% in 2021. In the same timeframe the number of wage and salary workers who belonged to unions increased 1.9% or 273,000 workers. The total number of workers belonging to unions in 1983, according to BLS was around 20.1%, nearly double what it is today.Acting US Labor Secretary Julie Su told Yahoo Finance on Friday that the White House does not plan to intervene in the UPS situation.“I have faith that the parties are going to find a path and continue to try to work things out,” she said Friday.Jennifer Schonberger, Josh Shafer and Jared Mitovich contributed to this report.Click here for the latest stock market news and in-depth analysis, including events that move stocksRead the latest financial and business news from Yahoo Finance]

Title: US labor secretary sees no need now to step into UPS-Teamsters talks
Text: [By Kanishka Singh and Nandita BoseWASHINGTON (Reuters) -Acting U.S. Labor Secretary Julie Su said on Friday she does not see a need at this stage to step in to urge parties to reach a deal in contract talks between the Teamsters Union and United Parcel Service."That is right," Su said on CNN when asked if she felt there was no need for her to intervene at this stage. She added she expected the parties to respect the bargaining process.On Wednesday, the Teamsters said UPS "walked away" from negotiations over a new contract. The company denied that and accused the union of stopping negotiating.On Friday, White House spokesperson Karine Jean-Pierre told reporters that President Joe Biden's administration was in contact with both sides and remained optimistic they would reach an agreement."I don't have any information on increased administration involvement, but certainly we remain in contact with both parties," Jean-Pierre said.The sides have traded salvos in statements as they try to avoid a strike when the current contract, which covers some 340,000 workers, expires at the end of July.If talks break down, UPS workers have already authorized a strike that would be their first since 1997. That strike lasted 15 days, cost the company $850 million, and sent some customers to rivalsBoth union and company officials have said they want a deal to prevent a strike, which could put millions of daily deliveries at risk.After missing out on wage increases during the pandemic, unions are aggressively seeking higher pay and better working conditions, pushing back on contract offers from companies grappling with labor shortages.Su recently helped negotiate a crucial contract deal between U.S. West Coast seaport employers and a union representing 22,000 workers.(Reporting by Kanishka Singh and Nandita Bose in Washington; Editing by David Holmes and David Gregorio)]

Title: Consultant: Strike could cost UPS 30% of diverted volume
Text: [UPS could see 30% of diverted volume disappear, consultant says (Photo: Jim Allen/FreightWaves)UPS Inc. should be prepared to lose as much as 30% of diverted volume should the Teamsters strike the company by the end of the month and a work stoppage last for a decent duration, a leading parcel consultant said Monday.UPS handled about 18.6 million parcels in the U.S. per day in the first quarter. Under a contingency plan, it expects to handle 4 million parcels on its own. The balance of about 14.6 million parcels, most of which would be ground deliveries, would be subject to diversion.Satish Jindel, president of consultancy ShipMatrix, said in a communique to FreightWaves that the 30% of volume that could be lost would be equivalent to more than 4 million parcels a day.Because there are about 80,000 package car drivers and each driver delivers about 230 parcels per day, the diverted volume, if it never returns to UPS (NYSE: UPS), could result in 4,300 lost driver jobs and those of a few thousand package handlers for every 1 million packages diverted, he said.Unlike the last Teamster strike in 1997, there is plenty of competition for diverted volume. For example, FedEx Corp., (NYSE: FDX) whose ground unit didn’t exist back then, is delivering on-time performance for air and ground on par with UPS, according to Jindel. This will give shippers more confidence to keep diverted volumes with FedEx, he said.On Sunday, the U.S. Postal Service launched “Ground Advantage” with two-to-five-day transit times comparable to FedEx and UPS. Jindel envisioned a scenario in which large shippers divert lightweight parcels under 5 pounds that can fit in a mailbox to the Postal Service and the heavier parcels to FedEx.The potential damage to UPS and its unionized workers behooves both sides to return to the table and resume negotiations, Jindel said. Talks collapsed last week reportedly over an inability to come to terms on part-time wages. No new talks are scheduled. The current contract expires July 31.“Being very tough in negotiations is analogous to stretching a rubber band,” Jindel wrote. “No one knows the full limit before it snaps and then one has to start all over again with a new set of conditions.”Story continuesSeparately, for the minority of Teamsters union members at UPS who don’t favor a strike should a contract not be agreed to in three weeks, the National Right to Work Legal Defense Foundation on Monday issued some advice.All UPS employees can resign their membership in the union and continue to do their jobs, according to a legal notice issued by the foundation. “If you don’t support the union you can send the union a letter resigning your membership at any time,” the notice said.In addition, employees who resign their membership — or who are already nonmembers — have the right to work even if the union orders a strike. “Union officials can — and often do — fine union members thousands of dollars for working during a strike,” the notice said. “So you should seriously consider resigning your union membership before you return to work during a strike, which is the only way to avoid fines and discipline.”Employees working in a “right-to-work” state, where union membership and financial support are voluntary, can resign their membership and opt out of all union financial support, according to the notice.Employees not working in a state with those protections have the right to opt out of paying dues for union politics and may be able to avoid other union financial support, according to the notice. In non-right-to-work states, unions can still only mandate that employees pay dues as a condition of employment if the union and management have finalized a union monopoly bargaining contract that contains a valid forced-dues clause, the notice said.About 97% of UPS’ members have voted to authorize a strike if a contract is not reached by July 31. The Teamsters represent 340,000 UPS employees, many of them part-timers.The post Consultant: Strike could cost UPS 30% of diverted volume appeared first on FreightWaves.]

Title: U.S. Postal Service Wants More Packages to Wrest Business From UPS, FedEx
The threat of a UPS strike is testing the strength of the labor market
Text: [The threat of a strike from 340,000 United Parcel Service (UPS) workers offers a new test of a recent surge in union power. It could also answer some questions about the strength of the larger US labor market.The unionized workforce at UPS was a big advantage for the package carrier earlier in the pandemic as demand for deliveries surged and rivals that lacked a steady supply of labor struggled to find enough available workers.But now that job gains are slowing and demand is cooling in some parts of the economy, it is less clear how much longer labor will hold the upper hand, either at UPS or the economy at large.New data released Friday by the Bureau of Labor Statistics showed the labor market is still tight, as the US economy added 209,000 jobs in June. That was the 30th straight month the US economy created jobs. Hourly wages also rose 4.4% over the same month last year, while the unemployment rate fell to 3.6%.But the data also showed some softening. Friday’s report marked the first in 15 months that job creation came in below what Wall Street economists had expected, reflecting a slowdown from the previous month.In the part of the economy where UPS operates — transportation and warehousing — employment actually dropped by 7,000 jobs in June.The labor market is cooling from "from overheated to lukewarm," Nancy Vanden Houten, lead US economist at Oxford Economics, said in a note on Friday.The direction of the labor market is important to the Federal Reserve as it decides whether to keep raising interest rates as a way of bringing down inflation. Officials at the central bank are watching for signs that companies are reducing hiring and wages.New wave of union activismPay is still a major issue for the International Brotherhood of Teamsters, which is pressing UPS to meet its demands for a new five-year collective bargaining agreement. It wants higher wages for the carrier’s part-time workers, among other benefits.Story continues"We need to drive up the starting rates of pay," Sean O’Brien, general president of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters, said this week on CNN.UPS has said it already offers industry-leading pay, with delivery drivers earning up to $42 per hour after four years on the job.On Wednesday, the Teamsters said the company failed to come to the table with an acceptable offer. Workers have authorized a strike to begin August 1 should no deal be reached.Sean O’Brien, general president of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters. REUTERS/Aude GuerrucciThe approach of the Teamsters is the latest sign of a new wave of union activism that took hold during the pandemic as demand for labor surged.Over the past week, Teamsters workers have expanded strikes against Amazon for delivery drivers in California and New York.The union is also testing Yellow, the nation’s third largest trucking company, to stick to the contract negotiated for its 22,000 union workers despite the company’s request to modify the agreement in efforts to avoid another bankruptcy.Amazon (AMZN), which runs its own shipping service, Amazon Logistics, has been facing unionization efforts from its warehouse workers in several states, while Apple (APPL) and Starbuck (SBUX) have been countering union pressure from retail workers.Is this 'a temporary or fundamental change'?Strikes that can jolt the nation’s supply chains are economic risks that the Biden administration has proven it is not willing to take.Over the past year, the administration has intervened in the dispute between West Coast Ports and the Dockworkers Union, and tapped Congress to settle differences between railroad companies and a dozen unions backing railway conductors. It is also monitoring talks between the auto companies and the United Auto Workers.Julie Su, acting Labor Secretary, said the White House does not plan to intervene in the UPS talks. (AP Photo/Alex Brandon, File)"All of a sudden we find ourselves in a situation we really haven’t experienced for some time," labor and employment expert and Penn State University law professor Paul Clark told Yahoo Finance."The big question is whether this is a temporary or fundamental change between unions and employers. We are trying to answer that right now, and it’s pretty difficult to say."Wayne State University labor law professor Michael Oswalt said even small disruptions in transportation, shipping and warehousing can be devastating across multiple industries. Still, he said, absent changes to labor law, which governs union campaigns and elections, unions are unlikely to regain the power they once had."So today what can matter more than a union’s size is its proximity to a company’s choke-point – and especially its willingness to strike," Oswalt said. "UPS Teamsters know the value they bring to the company, to the broader economy, and they have a history of pulling off successful strikes. That trifecta equates to a lot of union power right now."In January, the BLS reported that 10.1% of wage and salary workers belonged to unions in 2022, down from 10.3% in 2021. In the same timeframe the number of wage and salary workers who belonged to unions increased 1.9% or 273,000 workers. The total number of workers belonging to unions in 1983, according to BLS was around 20.1%, nearly double what it is today.Acting US Labor Secretary Julie Su told Yahoo Finance on Friday that the White House does not plan to intervene in the UPS situation.“I have faith that the parties are going to find a path and continue to try to work things out,” she said Friday.Jennifer Schonberger, Josh Shafer and Jared Mitovich contributed to this report.Click here for the latest stock market news and in-depth analysis, including events that move stocksRead the latest financial and business news from Yahoo Finance]
